vignette:
Margaret is a 73-year-old forester who has spent decades managing a large tract of state forest in the Pacific Northwest. Now retired on paper, she still volunteers with the local ranger station, though she can no longer tolerate the isolation she once loved. Her childhood was shaped by a mother who beat her unpredictably—fists, wooden spoons, whatever was at hand—usually when they were alone in the house. What Margaret remembers most vividly is not the pain but the silence that preceded it: the sudden hush of her mother’s footsteps stopping outside her door, the moment when all sound drained from the room, leaving only her own heartbeat. That silence still catches her off guard, even now, half a century later.

In the decades that followed, Margaret built a life around the unshakeable belief that her life was destroyed long ago, that she had become something less than human—an object to be acted upon. This core sense of dehumanization made her certain that no one could be trusted, that harm could come from anyone, at any time. She came to believe that the only way to survive was to stay in control of her environment, especially who she was alone with. Female coworkers and neighbors unsettled her most; she could not explain why, but being left in a room with a woman—even a kind one—made her feel like a small child again, waiting for the blow. She began to avoid such situations reflexively.

As the years passed, these appraisals shaped her daily choices. The fear that anyone might harm her—and the deep certainty that she was already ruined—drove her to adopt strategies that seemed to offer protection. She avoided exercise entirely, because the feeling of being out of breath, of her body working hard, reminded her of the helplessness she felt as a child pinned down. Spending money impulsively became her main comfort: buying new gear, tools, or clothes gave her a fleeting sense of agency and distraction from the emptiness. Most of all, she avoided being alone in any building or room—yet her job as a forester often required solitary patrols. She started volunteering only for group projects, even if that meant driving an hour to join a team, because the alternative felt unbearable.

But these strategies only deepened her negative appraisals. Each time she spent money she could not afford, she told herself that her life really was destroyed, that she was beyond repair. Each time she avoided a quiet trail or turned down a solitary task, she reinforced the belief that she was weak, an object at the mercy of her own fear. And her avoidance of exercise left her feeling physically frail, which she interpreted as further proof that the trauma had taken everything from her. The cycle tightened: the more she avoided, the more destroyed she felt; the more destroyed she felt, the more sensitive she became to triggers. She began to notice every sudden silence in the forest—a bird stopping mid-song, wind dying down—and her heart would race. She could not be near women without scanning for threat. The strategies that were meant to keep her safe made her world smaller and more dangerous.

Now, at 73, Margaret has exhausted her capacity for coping alone. She sought help after a panic attack in the ranger station break room when the coffee machine stopped making noise and a female volunteer asked if she was okay. She could not stay in the room. What frightens her most is the possibility that she will never feel whole again, that the object she feels like is all she has ever been. But she is also quietly hopeful that naming the silence—the one from childhood—might finally rob it of its power.
